content: The water authority has adopted a bottom-up strategy to address regulatory gaps by creating its own interim Drinking Water Regulatory Guidance and Compliance Standards. These standards encompass various aspects, including the withdrawal and protection of source water, treatment and distribution requirements, operator certification, and monitoring and reporting protocols, among other critical topics. The water authority has also successfully engaged Indigenous Services Canada, through the First Nations and Inuit Health Branch, to collaborate with Nova Scotia Environment and Climate Change. This partnership aims to provide interim support until First Nations can establish their own regulatory framework. This collaboration includes conducting third-party reviews of the water authority’s adherence to the Drinking Water Regulatory Guidance and Compliance Standards, analyzing drinking water quality test results, and offering environmental public health guidance to address any adverse findings in water quality tests. While this initiative primarily serves as a review and advisory function, it lays a crucial foundation for future legally mandated regulatory activities. The Government of Canada acknowledges the importance of involving the Atlantic First Nations Water Authority and other service providers in shaping regulations and standards. This involvement ensures that the requirements are practical and balanced with programs and tools that facilitate and encourage compliance. In Ireland, approximately 11% of the population relies on private water supplies, which are exempt from national drinking water regulations. These supplies typically serve single households for drinking and domestic purposes. The Environmental Protection Agency, which oversees public water supplies in Ireland, recommends that private well owners routinely conduct sanitary inspections to ensure the safety of their water and test water quality at least annually. These recommendations are supported by resources aimed at raising awareness and providing technical assistance to private well owners. In South Africa, the Blue Drop certification program, introduced in 2008 by the Department of Water and Sanitation, serves as an incentive-based regulatory mechanism for drinking water service providers. A similar program, the Green Drop, was established for wastewater services. The Blue Drop program uses rewards and penalties to drive behavioral changes, promote continuous improvement in drinking water services, encourage the adoption of best management practices, and ensure regulatory compliance. The program evaluates water suppliers based on key performance areas, which have evolved over time. For the 2021–2022 audit period, these areas included capacity management, drinking water quality risk management (via water safety planning), financial management, technical management, and drinking water compliance. Bonus points were awarded for process control training, performance agreements, public reporting of water quality results, and water demand management. Conversely, points were deducted for data discrepancies and failures to report drinking water quality issues. The program leverages reputational incentives, such as public performance reporting and benchmarking, as well as awards ceremonies to recognize high-performing water systems. In Germany, the Federal Water Act mandates the designation of drinking water catchment protection areas by state authorities. Decrees issued for these areas define local protective measures, which may be supplemented by voluntary cooperative agreements between water suppliers and farmers. These agreements encourage compliance with protective measures and mitigate adverse impacts on farmers. They promote farming practices that prevent contamination of drinking water sources by pesticides, pathogens, and nitrates. Farmers receive expert advice on techniques and practices to safeguard water resources through consultations, site visits, and informational materials. Topics covered include fertilization regimes, manure use, erosion control, and pesticide management. In some cases, program costs are funded by abstraction fees from licensing programs. For example, in Lower Saxony, at least 40% of abstraction fees are allocated to finance protective measures like cooperative agreements. Smaller water suppliers have merged to form larger subregional cooperatives to meet eligibility thresholds for cooperative agreement financing. In the Philippines, the Department of Health revised the Philippine National Standards for Drinking Water in 2017. These standards apply to all water supplies nationwide. The revision was driven by the need to integrate the 2014 national policy requiring water safety plans and address non-compliance issues with previous water quality monitoring requirements. The earlier standards were deemed too burdensome, particularly for small water suppliers with limited resources or access to accredited testing laboratories. The revised standards adopt a risk-based approach, categorizing parameters and prioritizing them for monitoring based on health risks and local occurrence. Parameters are grouped into three categories: mandatory, primary, and secondary. Mandatory parameters, such as Escherichia coli and disinfectant residuals, must be monitored by all water suppliers. These parameters were selected for their direct impact on health and their prevalence at concerning levels across the Philippines. The revised standards also allow for reduced monitoring frequency for certain parameters if three years of data show undetectable levels of the contaminant. In the Lao People’s Democratic Republic, the 2014 revision of national drinking water quality standards set an arsenic limit of 10 µg/L for urban water supplies. However, recognizing the limited treatment capacity of rural water supplies, an interim limit of 50 µg/L was established for five years, after which the limit was reduced to 10 µg/L for rural supplies as well. In Iceland, drinking water quality regulations establish tiered minimum monitoring requirements based on the population served by water supply facilities. Larger supplies are subject to more frequent testing. For example, systems serving 150 or fewer people require one test every two years, while those serving over 50,000 people require 34 tests annually, with an additional three tests for every 5,000 users beyond that threshold. The European Union’s Drinking Water Directive employs a risk-based approach to water quality monitoring requirements. Monitoring frequency and parameter lists may be reduced based on local risk assessments, provided certain conditions are met. For instance, monitoring frequency can be reduced if three years of data show concentrations below 60% of the parameter limit. Parameters can be removed from the monitoring list if concentrations remain below 30% of the limit over the same period, and risk assessments confirm no foreseeable factors that could degrade water quality. In Canada, field test kits are permitted for Escherichia coli testing in rural areas lacking access to accredited laboratories. Validated equipment must be used, and analysis should follow the manufacturer’s instructions. Presence-absence testing, which does not quantify organism concentrations, may be approved in some jurisdictions. Since the national limit for E. coli in drinking water is zero per 100 mL, any positive detection, regardless of quantity, is sufficient to prompt public health protection measures.
